newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian dodges police, assists another US suicide.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian dodges police, assists another US suicide.

text.p: Dodging police efforts to stop him, Dr. Jack Kevorkian on Saturday afternoon prevailed in his attempts to assist in the suicide of a 60-year-old California woman, his lawyer said.

Kevorkian drove the body of Isabel Correa, of Fresno, California, to William Beaumont Hospital in Royal Oak, Michigan, shortly after 2 p.m. on Saturday, said Colette Stimmell, a spokeswoman for the suburban Detroit hospital.

Geoffrey Fieger, Kevorkian's attorney, later read a statement to reporters that Correa had died in Kevorkian's presence, making it the 40th time the assisted suicide crusader has publicly acknowledged assisting a death.

Displaying a magenta sweater worn by Correa, who suffered from a painful spinal cord disorder, Fieger said she asked him to hold up the garment as "a flag of freedom that she was allowed to come here as a free suffering American to counsel with Dr. Kevorkian and end her suffering."
Correa's death capped an extraordinary 24 hours in the ongoing war between the assisted suicide crusader and local prosecutors.
At 7 p.m. on Friday, police disrupted a counselling session at a local hotel between Kevorkian and Correa, making it the first time in six years they halted a potential Kevorkian assisted suicide.
Acting on a tip from Correa's brother-in-law, Bloomfield Township police on Friday afternoon staked out the room rented by Correa and her husband at the Quality Inn.
Bloomfield Township Police Chief Jeffrey Werner said in a statement that officers saw Kevorkian and one of his supporters, Janet Good, enter the room with a covered box.
Six officers, some in uniform and others in plain clothes, asked permission to enter the room and were permitted after a short conversion with those inside, the police chief said.

After obtaining a search warrant, police searched the room and recovered "various containers which appeared to contain chemicals. Also recovered was a mechanical apparatus of the type used in assisted suicide incidents," Werner said in his statement.

But Kevorkian's lawyers offered a different version of events. Minutes after Kevorkian and Good had begun talking with Correa, between 20 and 30 police burst into the room after first using the ruse of "room service," they said.
They confiscated Correa's pain medication, her rosary and a sympathy card.

"If someone went in and did that without a uniform and a badge, you know what they'd call them? They'd call them burglars," Michael Schwartz, one of Kevorkian's legal team, said in an interview on Saturday.
Kevorkian plans to file charges that prosecutors and police violated his constitutional rights to privacy, Schwartz said.

People in motel rooms generally enjoy the same privacy protection as in their own homes, a constitutional law expert said on Saturday. However, police may enter uninvited if they believe someone's life is in danger, said Patrick Keenan, a law professor at University of Detroit Mercy.

Kevorkian has escaped conviction in three separate assisted-suicide trials involving five deaths. Last month, Oakland County Prosecutor Richard Thompson lost his bid for re-election, partly because of his unsuccessful attempts to put Kevorkian behind bars.

"This is Thompson's last gasp. A lot of tyrants do this when they are going out," Schwartz said. Thompson declined to comment on the possibility of a lawsuit on Saturday. He said police were obligated to act as they did.

Kevorkian's trials have left the legality of assisted suicide in Michigan unclear. Prosecutors claim it is a felony that violates the state's unwritten common law. But a jury acquitted Kevorkian on that charge, saying the law is unclear.
